questions.question: Distinguish urbanisation from urban growth, and rate of urbanisation from level of urbanisation, and explain how urban growth can occur without urbanisation.
questions.expected_answer: Urbanisation is the increasing percentage of a country's population living in urban areas — a proportion; urban growth is the increase in the actual number of urban residents — a headcount. Rate of urbanisation is the speed at which the urban percentage climbs, high in developing countries today; level of urbanisation is the percentage itself at a moment, high in developed countries — speed against snapshot. If urban and rural populations grow at the same pace, cities gain people (urban growth) while the urban percentage stands still, so there is growth without urbanisation.

questions.question: Explain the functional classification of towns, giving a South African example of a break-of-bulk point, a junction town, a gateway town, a gap town and two specialised towns.
questions.expected_answer: Functional classification sorts towns by their dominant work. A central place serves its surrounding sphere of influence with goods and services. A break-of-bulk point is where cargo transfers between transport modes and processing industry gathers — Richards Bay, where coal moves from trains into bulk carriers. A junction town grows where routes meet — De Aar at its railway junction. A gateway town controls entry between regions or countries — Komatipoort at the Mozambique border. A gap town commands a natural passage through mountains — Ceres or Tulbagh in the Cape Fold ranges. Specialised towns do one thing famously: Welkom (mining), Secunda (fuel-from-coal), Hermanus (tourism), Stellenbosch (education), Bhisho (administration).

questions.question: Describe the journey outward through a South African city's land-use zones, noting how apartheid planning deformed the residential pattern and what decentralised nodes have done to the CBD.
questions.expected_answer: The journey starts in the CBD — highest land values, tallest buildings, greatest accessibility, crowded by day and empty at night. Next comes the transition zone, a ring of mixed, changing land use: subdivided old houses, light industry, decay and gentrification together. Beyond lie the residential zones, in the classic model rising in income outward; apartheid deformed this by siting townships such as Mdantsane, Mamelodi and Gugulethu on the far urban edge behind buffer strips, railways and industrial belts, giving the poorest residents the longest, costliest commutes, with informal settlements attaching on the edges and along transport routes. Heavy industry follows railways, highways and harbours on flat land away from high-value housing, with light industrial parks near main roads and airports. Decentralised nodes such as Menlyn, uMhlanga Ridge and Canal Walk have drawn CBD functions out to the highways and high-income suburbs, contributing to the decline of some old centres and prompting urban renewal projects.
